title: Borrow Patterns Gallery
story: Every XIOM developer eventually hits the same borrow checker errors. But once you learn the patterns — read-only inspection, mutation, iteration, chaining — those errors become a distant memory.
why: Internalizing common borrow patterns eliminates guesswork — when you recognize the pattern, you already know the correct borrow to use.
analogy: Borrow patterns are like muscle memory for a pianist — you don't think about which finger to use anymore; your hands just move correctly.
try_it: Write a function that takes `&Ledger` and returns the average of all entries (sum / count). Add appropriate contracts. Then try making it take `&mut Ledger` instead — does the compiler allow you to call `inspect_all` afterward? Why or why not?
tips: Pattern 1 (&): Use for any function that answers a question about the data
Pattern 2 (&mut): Use for any function that changes the data — but only ONE at a time
Pattern 3 (iteration): Always &-borrow the collection; the loop variable is a copy of each element
Pattern 4 (chaining): &mut flows through the call chain — if one function needs it, all callers need it
common_mistakes: Trying to iterate while mutating — the borrow checker catches this at compile time
Using `&mut` for read-only operations — it prevents concurrent reads unnecessarily
Forgetting to chain the borrow — if `inner()` takes `&mut`, `outer()` must either take `&mut` or create the owned value
